Why it is here: Clear reporting on EU budget and Ukraine, with useful context

EU leaders seek agreement on long-term budget and Ukraine at summit

November 26, 2026

Leaders of the EU's 27 member states are expected to thrash out the EU's budget for 2028 to 2034. Ukraine and European Central Bank leadership are also up for discussion. DW has more.

What you need to know

- Special European Council meeting for the next two days

- Details of long-term budget, Ukraine's 2027 financial needs and ECB leadership on the agenda

- Euro Summit also taking place with outgoing ECB President Christine Lagarde

You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday 26th and Friday 27th November below:

EU budget from 2028 to 2034 and Ukraine funding on the agenda

European leaders are meeting for the next two days to thrash out a nearly €1.6 trillion ($1.76 trillion) budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.

The 27 member states are hoping to find common ground for a new budget proposal in the coming weeks and for members to agree on it at a summit on December 17 and 18.

"We, collectively, have the responsibility to find a balanced agreement that will allow the European Union to take on the challenges ahead: boosting our competitiveness, strengthening our security and defence and projecting Europe in the world," said President of the European Council Antonio Costa ahead of the talks.

Costa outlined three key objectives for the next two days:

- to achieve a balanced distribution of funds between the EU's strategic priorities,

- to keep national contributions within reasonable limits

- to include a balanced basket of own resources, including five new sources of EU revenue

Revenue would come from digital services, non-recycled e-waste, tobacco related products, the carbon border adjustment mechanism and the emissions trading system, according to a statement from the European Council.

Ukraine's financing needs for 2027 and beyond will also be dealt with during talks. Currently, €45 billion has been earmarked in additional financial support for Ukraine in 2027, building on the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027.

It's not expected to be a smooth process with Reuters quoting a diplomat as expecting "leaders to be yelling, complaining, showing they are willing to fight. They need that first. They need a breakdown, blood on the walls, before they can get to an agreement."

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the two-day Special European Council meeting in Brussels, which is expected to focus on the EU’s next long-term budget, support for Ukraine and then the leadership of the European Central Bank (ECB).

Leaders of the bloc's 27 members states will be looking to find common ground over the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 ahead of an expected deal in December.

Continued support for Ukraine in 2027 and beyond is up for discussion as Russia's invasion drags on towards a fifth year.

The question of who replaces European Central Bank chief Christine Lagarde is also on the agenda.

item.title: Wealthy Europeans look beyond stocks amid AI selloff. Here’s where they’re investing
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains AI investment trends among wealthy Europeans

Wealthy Europeans are looking to alternative asset classes to build exposure to artificial intelligence themes amid turbulence in public markets.

Goldman Sachs Alternatives' inaugural survey of high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth investors found 47% of European respondents saw alternatives as the best way to gain exposure to AI and future tech growth, compared to just 24% of U.S. investors.

The survey found a significant gap between the U.S. and Europe in terms of investor knowledge of alternatives, which include assets like private equity, property and infrastructure. Goldman said 82% of European respondents are familiar with the alternative investments market — compared to 50% of U.S. investors.

Goldman polled 1,000 investors with at least 1 million in investable assets in their local currency across the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland. The survey was carried out between June 29 and Aug. 18 this year.

The report on the findings, published Wednesday, did not specify the proportion of respondents who already have a stake in some kind of alternative investment — but wealthy Europeans appeared particularly bullish on the space.

Private equity made up the largest proportion of current alternatives holdings. Among wealthy Europeans with alternatives exposure, 62% said they invested in private equity. The second most commonly held asset class was private real estate, which was backed by 51% of European alternatives investors. Hedge funds were held by 37% of European alternatives owners, and private infrastructure was held by 30%.

One in four respondents who did not already own an alternative investment said they were likely to invest in the market in the coming 12 months. Among those already in the space, 26% said they were likely to increase their allocations over the next year, while just 5% said they planned to decrease their exposure.

Of the European investors who already owned alternatives, 54% said their assets had performed as expected, while 44% said their assets had exceeded their expectations to the upside. Only 2% said their alternative investments had performed worse than expected.

"Recent reforms gave individual investors unprecedented access to alternative asset classes like private equity, venture capital, and private credit," Kyle Kniffen, global head of alternatives for third-party wealth at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said in Wednesday's report.

He added that wealthy investors "look ready to jump at the opportunity."

"Our survey shows satisfaction among current alts owners is high and adoption looks set to increase," Kniffen said.

Alternative investments have increasingly become a staple of high-net-worth individuals' investment portfolios.

Over the past year, JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in the Asia-Pacific region have jumped 40%, while BNY Wealth says alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios — recently surpassing traditional assets for the first time.

But investing in alternatives carries risks. Private equity, for example, can lock up capital for long periods, and although the number of exits ticked slightly higher last year, the value of those deals fell.

Concerns about private credit, meanwhile, have dominated headlines, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warning on Oct. 14, 2025, that "cockroaches" were likely to be lurking in private markets.

— CNBC's Lee Ying Shan contributed to this article.

Why it is here: Detailed analysis of US tariffs and international response

'Unacceptable': Major economies push back against new US tariffs

China, the European Union and other major trading partners on Thursday criticised new US tariffs of up to 20 percent proposed by US President Donald Trump after a probe into alleged global overcapacity, raising the prospect of fresh trade tensions with allies and rivals alike.

Major economies from China to the EU hit out at proposed new US tariffs after Washington concluded its months-long probe into alleged excess production, potentially opening a new phase in trade tensions with both allies and foes alike.

The new tolls, which follow an investigation launched days after the Supreme Court struck down US President Donald Trump's previous duties, range up to 20 percent and face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.

Read moreTrump announces new tariffs on EU, China despite US midterms defeat

The levies target some of the United States' largest trading partners, with China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam in the crosshairs.

Some, such as Japan, denied having excessive production.

"Japan does not have any non-market policy practices or structural excess production capacity... It is regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced in spite of this," the country's top government spokesman Minoru Kihara said.

A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the proposals sought to take existing trade deals into account.

China is among those facing a 20-percent tariff, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.

"China understands that we're going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding," he told US broadcaster CNBC, adding that Washington was offering China exemptions on around $30 billion of goods.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

'Real concern'

The European Union said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the United States to stick by a deal struck last year.

"The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action," European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said.

China's foreign ministry, responding to a question about the new levies before they were officially announced, warned Washington not to engage in "tariff wars and trade wars."

Watch moreEU says 'strongly' rejects premise of new US tariffs

And Singapore said on Thursday it was "very disappointed" with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidizing manufacturing.

Vietnam also faces a 20-percent tariff; Cambodia and Indonesia 18 percent; and India 17 percent, according to the USTR's office.

The EU, South Korea and Taiwan, which have signed trade deals with the United States, will see tariffs broadly capped at 15 percent.

In a separate announcement, the USTR also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.

The Brazilian president's office called the measures "unacceptable" and said Brasilia would "not yield to this type of threat."

Trump's tariffs have targeted Washington's friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in the country.

Overcapacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement and chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said.

Watch moreTrump's tariffs hitting US small businesses

'Hollowing out'

The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on expenses to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.

Affordability was a key issue in this month's US midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party swept out of power in both chambers of Congress by Democrats.

The announcement came as data showed the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge at a three-year high in October, adding to pressure to hike interest rates.

Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus said that he expected this probe to be among "the most important" actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and "never get turned off, even if there's no demand."

This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a "hollowing out" of US manufacturing, he added.

While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact.

The new levies will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.

In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labor.

For economies facing both the forced labor and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack up and the higher rate will prevail, the US official said.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Why it is here: Reports on India's stance in trade talks with the US

India news: Resolve tariff concerns in trade talks — India tells US

November 26, 2026

India has denied US claims that New Delhi's policies promote excess manufacturing capacity. Further headlines from India include Constitution Day celebrations. DW has more.

What you need to know

Here are the latest developments from India on Thursday, November 26:

- New Delhi urges US to work out trade-related within the structures of the ongoing trade deal talks

- India celebrates Constitution Day

- India observes 18th anniversary of deadly 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks

India seeks 'early conclusion' of trade deal with US

In its statement on planned new US tariffs, India's commerce ministry urged the US to resolve trade disputes and complete negotiations over a new trade deal.

The ministry said that it was "committed to working closely" with the US towards an "early conclusion" of the trade deal.

The US proposed a tariff rate of 25% on goods from India, reduced to 17% if a trade deal is reached.

The state of India-US trade deal negotiations

US President Donald Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi first announced talks for the US-India Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) last year.

But negotiations were delayed over strained ties and global conflict, reestablishing headway only this year.

The two nations released the framework for an interim trade agreement in February. As part of that deal, India would "eliminate or reduce tariffs" on all US industrial products and a range of US food and agricultural goods.

However, the negotiations for a final deal were once again stalled after the US Supreme Court invalidated much of Trump's sweeping global tariffs.

In October, India's Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman described the talks as having reached "a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult."

But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a few days later that New Delhi and Washington were "about asclose as you can be without having an executed agreement."

India rejects US charge of excess capacity

Facing a new United States tariff threat, India has stressed that any trade concerns be addressed within the framework of the ongoing trade deal talks between the two countries.

New Delhi's statement comes after Washington on Wednesday unveiled a new wave of tariffs on 14 of its major trade partners, including India, claiming that the economies were promoting excess industrial capacity.

"India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement. It has been India's position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations," a statement from New Delhi's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said late Wednesday.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced new import duties of 20% to 40% to counter the alleged excessive manufacturing abroad as it completed a monthslong probe into alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.

The new tariffs will be subject to a period of public comment before taking effect.

"Today, after lengthy investigations, Ambassador Greer has determined that the acts, policies, and practices of various economies designed to artificially support manufacturing exports are unreasonable and burden or restrict US commerce and has proposed responsive action," the USTR said on Wednesday.

The USTR said that it will reduce the tariff rate for Indian imports to 17% if a trade deal is sealed between New Delhi and Washington in the long-drawn-out talks trade negotiations between the two sides.

India said that it had "engaged constructively" throughout USTR's investigation and said that it did not have "structural excess capacity in any sector."

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's bureau in New Delhi, back with our daily India news blog — where we break down all the biggest headlines that have grabbed the attention of the world's most populous democracy.

This Thursday marks 77 years since India officially adopted its Constitution. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has extended his greetings on the occasion and political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party has planned a "Save Democracy, Save Constitution" rally.

After the US proposed raising levies on 14 of its trading partners, including in India, over alleged excess industrial capacity, New Delhi has called for the trade concerns to be addressed through the ongoing talks of a trade deal with Washington. India has also rejected having structural overcapacity in any sector.

Stay tuned as we bring you all this and more.

item.title: War and drought threaten livelihoods of Sudan’s farmers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Focuses on the impact of war and drought on Sudan's farmers

War and drought threaten livelihoods of Sudan’s farmers

Attacks on electricity infrastructure and drought are threatening Sudan’s harvests and leaving millions without water.

Haider Mohamed has worked as a farmer in Sudan’s Northern State for more than 40 years, growing fava beans, wheat, and a variety of seasonal crops.

But Sudan’s water crisis – a combination of lower-than-average rainfall and war-induced devastation to infrastructure – has severely affected his harvest and his income.

It’s a situation Mohamed describes as unprecedented in his 40 years of farming.

Mohamed owns a small farm covering about four hectares (about 10 acres) in al-Saleem, near the city of Dongola. He keeps part of his harvest to feed his family, and then sells the rest at local markets to cover essential living expenses, including healthcare and his children’s education.

“Our crops were destroyed last year, and this year it is difficult to generate any income because we are still facing electricity and irrigation problems,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera, referring to drone attacks on power stations that disrupted electricity supplies, and regularly stopped him from using electricity-dependent irrigation systems. “We have accumulated a lot of debt, and we fear that we will not harvest enough to feed our children, let alone have any surplus to sell in the market.”

Mohamed’s experience is far from unique. Across Northern State and other parts of Sudan, water shortages caused by declining rainfall or disruptions to irrigation are increasingly threatening agricultural production and the livelihoods of farming communities.

“Those who rely on diesel-powered pumps [for irrigation] cannot find fuel, and when it is available, it is extremely expensive,” Mohamed explained. “We also cannot afford the cost of installing solar-powered irrigation systems. At this rate, no one will be able to continue farming in this country.”

The ongoing war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in 2023, has severely disrupted fuel supplies in the country. Attacks on Sudan’s largest oil refinery, as well as fuel depots and petrol stations, have exacerbated shortages.

In just October, attacks blamed on the RSF damaged critical infrastructure across 11 states, disrupting electricity and water services and disabling several water supply sources.

Rising global energy prices have also made imports more expensive, with the United Nations reporting that the price of diesel nearly doubled between March and August this year.

Struggle to find drinking water

In Sudan’s rain-fed agricultural regions, drought has compounded the problems facing farmers.

Rainfall during this year’s June-to-September rainy season declined across most of Sudan’s agricultural areas, believed to be linked to the ongoing global El Nino phenomenon. In the southeastern states of Gedaref and Sennar, rainfall was approximately 30 percent and 20 percent compared with normal levels, respectively, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

The two states normally account for about a quarter of Sudan’s sorghum production – the country’s main staple cereal.

The impact of the water crisis extends beyond the agricultural sector, affecting millions of people struggling to access drinking water and meet their basic household needs.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) says damage to water and electricity systems and other civilian infrastructure has deprived millions of people of essential services, while disruptions to water supplies have increased the risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases.

The UN children’s agency, UNICEF, estimates that more than 27 million people in Sudan are in need of water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance.

Between January and June of this year, UNICEF and its partners provided 6.6 million people with access to safe water, with approximately two-thirds of those receiving emergency assistance, including displaced people, those who had returned home and communities affected by conflict and cholera.

In the capital Khartoum, residents are still forced to stand in long queues for water, sometimes waiting for hours. Widespread disruptions to water supply networks and the shutdown of several water stations due to damage sustained during the war have left many households without a reliable water supply.

Saleh Zaki, who lives in Khartoum State’s East Nile district, said the area has suffered from water supply problems for many years, even before the outbreak of the war.

“Before the war, we repeatedly sought help from the authorities, only to be told there was no budget to address the problem,” Zaki said. “We therefore raised funds ourselves and hired a specialist to drill two wells, providing residents with limited water supply.”

“Since the conflict damaged the water networks … we urgently need more wells, repairs to the supply networks and solar-powered systems to support our neighbourhood and nearby communities,” he added.

Solar power

In August, the Sudanese government announced a series of measures designed to ease the water crisis and encourage families displaced by war to return home.

These measures include exempting solar panels imported for personal use from customs duties, taxes, and other government fees, and waiving residential water fees nationwide until the end of 2026.

However, these measures remain limited in their impact unless accompanied by broader economic policies.…

item.description:

Why it is here: Discusses EU budget and Ukraine funding, with political context

EU leaders face showdown over Ukraine funding as divisions deepen

European Union leaders on Thursday are set to tackle deep divisions as they meet in Brussels to discuss the bloc's long-term budget in Brussels, which includes a proposed €45 billion loan to keep Ukraine funded through 2027.

European Union (EU) leaders will seek on Thursday to bridge major differences over the bloc’s long-term budget and agree on a significant new loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.

The new joint budget is a statement of the EU’s ambitions in the world and is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies. The 2028-2034 package could amount to between 1% and 1.2% of the bloc’s gross national income.

“The time has come to reach an agreement,” European Council President António Costa wrote in a summit invitation letter. Last weekend, he tabled a new proposal to solve the budget riddle, cutting about 10% off the original European Commission plan.

Costa, who will chair the two-day meeting in Brussels, said that leaders have “the responsibility to find a balanced agreement that will allow the European Union to take on the challenges ahead.”

Complicating things are upcoming elections in France, Italy and Poland next year and in Spain on Sunday. The hard right leads in surveys in France and winners in Poland and Spain are tough to predict. New governments could make it even harder to agree on a deal next year if one isn't found by the end of next month.

The EU is divided into hard-to-move camps when it comes to the budget. They’re getting even tougher to budge as Europe’s debt strife spreads and countries are forced into greater defense spending over Russia’s almost five-year-long war on Ukraine.

Around a third of countries are so-called net contributors that pay in more than they get back in allocations. Germany, Austria, the Netherlands and Sweden are the most vocal in their opposition to being asked to cough up even more and demand belt-tightening.

A large group of countries, led by France and Italy and dubbed the “friends of cohesion,” staunchly defends funds that protect farmers and pay for infrastructure projects in relatively poor member countries, to help bring them up to EU standards.

Those policies make up about two thirds of the entire budget.

But most countries also want to direct spending to new areas, as the EU confronts challenges like supporting Ukraine as it fights off a Russian invasion and remaining competitive in the face of high energy prices and trade tensions with the US and China.

It would be drawn from online advertising and money that companies make from user data and could amount to 5 billion euros ($5.5 billion) a year.

Ukraine is a big part of the budget puzzle. The spending package foresees a 100 billion-euro ($110 billion) envelope for Ukraine over seven years. The leaders must also decide on a new 45 billion-euro ($49.4 billion) loan for the country.

Earlier this month, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz threatened to hold up a budget agreement if there were no “collective commitment” made to Ukraine by all member countries, “without exception.”

Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using funds for military aid to Ukraine. In a letter to Costa, Merz said that helping “Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support.”

Nearly a year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of 90 billion euros ($99 billion) to cover most of the Ukrainian government's needs for two years. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are straining Ukraine’s finances.

item.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Reports on SpaceX's plan for space-based data centers

FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical

The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" (forming a data center constellation called "Starmind") would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing "the full power of the sun."

"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier."

A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least "one authorized space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.

Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy."

"It's not going to happen," he said Wednesday.

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun's energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.

He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.

"You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions," said Becker, noting such crashes could create "a cloud of debris" in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.

In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a "substantial number" of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest" — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.

The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.

In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky."

"The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that "these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky."

Becker echoed that sentiment. "It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye," he said.

Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' requests for further comment Wednesday.

item.title: The world must choose between nuclear abolition and nuclear catastrophe
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Opinion piece on nuclear abolition and the risk of nuclear catastrophe

The world must choose between nuclear abolition and nuclear catastrophe

The upcoming UN nuclear ban treaty conference offers an opportunity to challenge the dogma of nuclear deterrence.

The world is currently facing the greatest risk of deliberate or inadvertent nuclear conflict since the Cold War – or perhaps ever.

While the threat of nuclear war may have dropped out of the headlines, it did not go away with the end of the Cold War. The United States and Russia had a window of opportunity in the early 1990s to eliminate nuclear weapons when there were still only 5 nuclear powers, but they spurned it.

Fast forward to today, and these two countries that, between them, possess almost 90 percent of the world’s nuclear weapons have initiated wars with non-nuclear-armed countries: Ukraine and Iran. The aggressors’ leaders, presidents Putin and Trump, have made threats to use nuclear weapons.

It is worrying that while these threats have not gone unreported, they have quickly passed from the headlines. However, the good news is that the rest of the world is pushing back against this ongoing existential threat – not through mass protests, but through quiet, multilateral diplomacy and persistent advocacy by civil society, including my organisation, ICAN.

Putin and Trump did recently meet their Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, who commands the third-largest nuclear arsenal, for their first-ever three-way summit. They reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. But in their declaration, they did not say anything new; simply that they would discuss reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

The question we face today of how we ensure our security in a world of newly competing nuclear-armed powers is, at its root, the same we have faced since the development of the atomic bomb – how do we deal with the constant threat these weapons pose to humanity?

Despite the insistence of the nuclear-armed minority that there is no alternative to their theory of nuclear deterrence, we are part of a diplomatic push offering the world a choice. Powerful countries can continue to blindly believe in deterrence dogma, a theory of human behaviour unsupported by evidence, that has led us to the brink of catastrophe more than once. Or countries can agree to the total elimination of these weapons for good.

Deterrence is based on the capability and willingness to use nuclear weapons to kill millions of innocent people. The threat is present every moment in the form of the 4,000 nuclear weapons deployed and ready to use at short notice – more than enough to end civilisation as we know it many times over. This is the current choice of a minority of countries – the nine that have nuclear weapons and their nuclear-endorsing allies, principally the members of NATO.

The alternative of abolishing nuclear weapons is growing in strength, but not talked about nearly as much. It is the choice of the majority of the world and is embodied in the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons – the United Nations’ nuclear ban treaty, or TPNW, that 101 countries have already signed or ratified.

The treaty bans nuclear weapons and all activities associated with them outright and has created a new norm of international law that makes these weapons unacceptable, alongside biological and chemical weapons.

The first review conference of the treaty will soon take place at the UN in New York under the presidency of South Africa – a country that set the example of how nuclear weapons can be eliminated by doing it. In the 1970s, Apartheid South Africa, with the help of Israel, developed a nuclear arsenal, but then voluntarily dismantled it under international supervision in the 1990s.

The conference will evaluate how the treaty has been implemented so far and identify how it can be further strengthened. Unlike the review conference of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty earlier this year that failed to reach consensus for the third consecutive time, this gathering is expected to agree on a number of significant decisions. There will be a strong political declaration stressing the importance of nuclear disarmament and the urgency of addressing the growing risk that nuclear weapons could be used again in conflict, including calling out the role of nuclear deterrence in driving this threat to all countries. There is also the prospect of more countries using the conference as an opportunity to sign or ratify the treaty.

As TPNW states have noted, deterrence does not bring security and stability; it brings chronic insecurity to the entire world. There is nothing inevitable about nuclear weapons. They are a political choice. They are created by human hands, and they can be dismantled by human hands – as South Africa demonstrated.

The remaining countries that support the treaty but still need to join it should do so now. That will highlight just how isolated the nine nuclear-armed countries are and add to the pressure on them and their allies to get on the right side of history.

The words of President Kennedy addressing the UN 65 years ago remain as relevant today: “The weapons of war must be abolished before they abolish us.”
